results.corrected_extracted: US commercial insurance claims, 2013–2015 (796,330 people aged 16–64): sustained gabapentin overuse without opioid overuse, against gabapentin without overuse, all-cause hospital admission OR 1.366 (95% CI 1.055–1.769) and drug-related admission 1.440 (1.010–2.053); sustained gabapentin overuse with sustained opioid overuse (comparison group not stated in the review), all-cause admission 4.083 (2.582–6.457) and emergency or inpatient care for respiratory depression 4.106 (1.753–9.619). Listed limitations include possible residual confounding and claims that may not reflect consumption; adjustment is not described.
results.note: Table 1 names the comparator (gabapentin alone without overuse) only for the first set; for the opioid-overuse set neither Table 1 nor 4.5 states it. All numbers match.
Reference 68 (Molero et al., BMJ 2019) lies outside the included references [6, 9–62] (PDF p. 2); the hazard ratios and the 'not specifically misusing' caveat match 4.5, 3rd paragraph.

results.corrected_extracted: The abstract concludes that evidence suggests gabapentinoid misuse is a growing trend causing significant patient harm (the Discussion, 4.6, states this without the hedge), and the Conclusion, also prefaced by 'evidence suggests', calls the trend alarming; the Discussion says the harm seen with gabapentinoids taken with opioids was not limited to people with substance use disorders or to misuse. Limitations: highly heterogeneous studies, hence a qualitative synthesis only; limited generalisability (small samples, single sites, a focus on substance use disorder or overdose cohorts rather than the general population); retrospective designs; reliance on surrogate markers of misuse and harm; and the assumption of a class effect, that findings for one gabapentinoid apply to the other.
results.note: Both the Abstract's and the Conclusion's statements begin 'Evidence suggests'; that hedge was dropped. 4.6 itself states the harm unhedged. Limitations otherwise match 4.7.

results.corrected_extracted: Core team: a chair (V. Favier), a vice-chair (L. Nitro) and a methodologist (A. M. Saibene), the last two the first and senior authors of the systematic review whose classification the panel adopted (statement 2.2, consensus, mean 8.44). The limitations call the study subjective and one involving only rhinologists, so effects of snorting on the dorsal septum, nasal pyramid or lips (aesthetic complaints) were not assessed, and say ENT specialists are not experts in the care of drug dependence, which belongs to addiction medicine. No statement is graded for the evidence behind it.

key_findings.correction: Motives reported: in Swedish opioid maintenance, relief of emotional problems 65%, getting high 27%, relief of physical problems 12%; in a German detoxification ward, easing opioid withdrawal (67.1% in the text, 61.7% in Table 1) or benzodiazepine withdrawal (6.3%), combining with other substances (51.9%), recreation (46.8%), curiosity (40.5%), mental health problems (13.9%) and pain (8.9%); among US people with opioid use disorder, reasons for first misuse of gabapentin were getting high (58.1%), limited access to their previous drug of choice (29%), boosting other drugs (29%), self-treating withdrawal (25.8%) and pain (16.1%). [Was 'no access to their usual drug'; the review says limited access, PDF pp. 7, 24.]

Australia: 1158 reports of intentional poisoning involving pregabalin, with a 53.8% yearly increase (95% CI 44.0–64.2%) from 2005 to 2016, and 88 pregabalin-associated deaths, of which 1.1% were attributed to pregabalin alone; pregabalin misuse-related ambulance attendances in Victoria rose from 0.28 to 3.32 per 100,000 from 2012 to 2017 (p=0.001), 67.6% with sedative co-ingestion (benzodiazepines 36.6%), and 39% of the attendances were for suicide attempts. [Table 1, PDF p. 9, says misuse-related and gives the 39%.]

FAERS reports, October 2012 to December 2016: 576 gabapentin and 58 pregabalin abuse, misuse, dependence or overdose reports, of which 18.4% and 41.4% were fatal (cause of death not determined); proportional reporting ratio for pregabalin against gabapentin 1.77. US studies point to more gabapentin than pregabalin misuse and European studies to more pregabalin misuse; the authors suggest ('presumably') that local prescribing differences may play a significant role. [4.1, 4th paragraph, PDF p. 21, hedges this.]

reporting_issues.correction: issue: For the German detoxification survey (Snellgrove et al. [38]), Table 1 gives the share whose main reason was relieving opioid withdrawal as 61.7%, while the Discussion gives 67.1%. | consequence: By the editors' arithmetic all seven of the Discussion's percentages for this survey fit a base of 79 (67.1% = 53/79, 51.9% = 41/79, 46.8% = 37/79, 40.5% = 32/79, 13.9% = 11/79, 8.9% = 7/79, 6.3% = 5/79), which 61.7% does not, so the table's 61.7% is the likelier transposition; this is inference, so cite the primary study.

reporting_issues.note: Checked in Bonnet & Scherbaum 2017, Table 1, PDF p. 5: baclofen 1.3% (19), gabapentin 1.1% (17), pregabalin 0.5% (8) of 1500; 13.1% (5) and 57.8% (22) fit a base of 38 = 2.5%.

risk_of_bias.note: Design systematic review, instrument AMSTAR 2 and overall critically low agreed (critical items 2, 4, 7, 9 and 13 unmet). Item 8 note: besides Macleod, Ianni and Mutschler have period 'unknown' and Buttram [56] and Chatterjee 'not listed'.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial agreed. Precision: the Abstract and Conclusion are prefaced 'Evidence suggests' (the card quotes only the clause), while 4.6 states the harm unhedged; the causal-language gap stands either way.

missed: Dahlman [17]: the motive (65/27/12%) and source (46/35/15%) percentages fit a base of 26, the 36% of 73 who had ever used pregabalin (17, 7, 3 and 12, 9, 4 of 26), not the 15 (21%) with nonmedical use that the text names (editors' arithmetic; PDF pp. 9, 24).

Daly [18] (Irish National Self-Harm Registry, 72,391 intentional drug overdoses, 2007–2015): the intent (self-harm or misuse) could not be told apart (Table 1, PDF p. 9); Table 1's crude 'admission more common' (49.4% vs 41.4%) becomes gabapentinoid involvement that 'increased hospitalisation risk' in 4.5, which also drops 'intentional' (PDF p. 27).

key_findings.correction: Remission was much lower for legal than for illegal drugs; the author argues that availability, including legal status, is the simplest explanation, citing history: after the 1914 Harrison Act, laudanum drinkers and opium smokers all but disappeared, the laudanum drinkers seeking treatment or somehow stopping rather than switching to heroin (less is known about the opium smokers), and in Canada a Prohibition-era rise in alcohol prices was followed by a deep dip in consumption and about a one-third drop in cirrhosis cases (Seeley, 1960, as summarized). [p. 49 says both groups all but disappeared; 'from the record' is not in the text.]

reporting_issues.note: Readings agree (panel a 18–29: about 57% and 71%; panel b: about 52%). Panel b's legend reads 'Drug dependence' while its caption says abuse/dependence, which may explain the gap; the card's 'if the panels describe the same cases' covers this.

Checked in Robins 1993: 6% of those positive at departure entered treatment (p. 1045), two-thirds of treated relapsed (p. 1046), 12% of those addicted in Vietnam re-addicted in 3 years (p. 1045), treated cases cannot stop on their own (p. 1050, from the Selective Service study).

risk_of_bias.note: Design narrative review, no applicable instrument, editors' checklist and overall high (worst domain) agreed.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial agreed; each step checked (Figure 4 cannabis line about 0.13 to 0.03; Robins 1993, p. 1051, 'few ... would have become addicted' in the US). Strictly, 'not a chronic relapsing disease' is in Summary Point 1 and p. 37, not the abstract.

missed: cannot_establish says treatment and remission 'were not related in these data' (citing p. 42), but p. 42 says only that the relation between treatment and remission in population samples had yet to be published, i.e. it was not tested; reword so it does not read as a null finding.
p. 43: where the surveys used the same remission criteria, rates 'hovered at about 80%' with an average absolute deviation of 2.7% (the author's summary of NCS, NCS-R and NESARC).

key_findings.correction: The highest-rated statement: patients should be correctly informed that no “safe threshold” of cocaine use prevents further evolution of the lesions (3.4, strong consensus, mean 8.89, range 8–9); they must also be advised that the only known way to halt lesion development is to stop nasal cocaine use (3.3, strong consensus, mean 8.61, range 7–9). The discussion supports both with one narrative review (ref. 31). [p. 12 names 3.4 and 1.2 (8.83) as the two top-scoring items; 3.3 is not the second, and 3.13, 3.14, 4.4 and 4.6 (8.72) also rate higher.]

Limitations stated by the authors: the subjective nature of the study; only rhinologists took part, so effects of snorting on the dorsal septum, nasal pyramid or lips (aesthetic complaints) were not assessed; ENT specialists are not experts in addiction; most people do not disclose their use and relapses are frequent. [4.5, p. 15, says 'dorsal septum', not nasal dorsum.]
